'''Lai-Sheng Wang''' ({{zh|s=王来生|t=王來生|p=Wáng Láishēng}}, born 1961) is a Chinese experimental physical chemist who formerly served as the chair of the Chemistry Department at [[Brown University]].<ref name="fac">{{cite web |url=https://www.brown.edu/academics/chemistry/people/faculty/lai-sheng-wang |title=Lai-Sheng Wang Faculty Page |publisher=Brown University |accessdate=2022-11-12 |archive-date=2023-10-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231013113451/https://www.brown.edu/academics/chemistry/people/faculty/lai-sheng-wang |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is known for his work on atomic gold pyramids and [[Boron trichloride|planar boron clusters]].

==Education==
Wang obtained a B.S. degree in chemistry from Wuhan University in 1982, and a Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1990. He completed his postdoctoral stay at [[Rice University]] before moving to [[Richland, Washington]] in 1993 to accept a joint position between [[Washington State University]] and [[Pacific Northwest National Laboratory]].

In 2009, he moved to Brown University, where he teaches [[physical chemistry]] and conducts research. He was named the Jesse H. and Louisa D. Sharpe [[Jesse H. Metcalf|Metcalf]] Professor of Chemistry in 2015 and chair of the Department in 2019.<ref name="fac"/>

==Research==
Throughout his career, Wang has predominately studied [[Nanoparticle|nanoclusters]] and solution-phase chemistry in the gas phase, focusing on the fundamental behaviors of nanoclusters using [[Photoemission spectroscopy|photoelectron spectroscopy]] and computational techniques. With his group,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://casey.brown.edu/chemistry/research/LSWang/ |title=Home - LS Wang Group |publisher=Casey.brown.edu |date= |accessdate=2013-11-20 |archive-date=2014-02-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140209221639/http://casey.brown.edu/chemistry/research/LSWang/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> he has discovered golden [[Buckminsterfullerene|bucky-balls]] and the smallest golden pyramid, as well as aromatic clusters and planar [[boron]] clusters. His group has pioneered spectroscopic studies in the gas-phase of free multiply-charged [[anion]]s and solution-phase molecules, such as metal complexes, [[redox]] species, and biologically-relevant molecules. His group has also developed ion-trap techniques to create ultracold anions that allow high resolution photoelectron spectroscopy to be performed on complex molecules.

In 2014, Wang's research team at [[Brown University]] showed that the structure of {{chem|B|36}} was not only possible but highly stable.<ref name="news.brown.edu">{{cite web|url=https://news.brown.edu/pressreleases/2014/01/borophene |title= New boron nanomaterial may be possible |publisher=Brown University |date=2014-01-27 |accessdate=2013-03-09}}</ref><ref name="spectrum.ieee.org">{{cite web|url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/borophene-might-be-joining-graphene-in-the-2d-material-club |title= 'Borophene' Might Be Joining Graphene in the 2-D Material Club |publisher=IEEE Spectrum |date=2014-01-28 |access-date=2013-03-09}}</ref><ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal|title= Planar hexagonal B36 as a potential basis for extended single-atom layer boron sheets |journal= Nature Communications |volume= 5 |article-number= 3113 |publisher=Nature |date=2014-01-20 |doi= 10.1038/ncomms4113 |pmid= 24445427 |last1= Piazza |first1= Zachary A. |last2= Hu |first2= Han-Shi |last3= Li |first3= Wei-Li |last4= Zhao |first4= Ya-Fan |last5= Li |first5= Jun |last6= Wang |first6= Lai-Sheng |bibcode= 2014NatCo...5.3113P |doi-access= free }}</ref> [[Photoelectron spectroscopy]] revealed a relatively simple spectrum, suggesting a symmetric cluster. Neutral B36 is the smallest boron cluster to have sixfold symmetry and a perfect hexagonal vacancy, and it can be viewed as a potential basis for extended two-dimensional boron sheets.<ref name=k1401>{{cite journal|url=http://www.kurzweilai.net/will-borophene-replace-graphene-as-a-better-conductor-of-electrons |title=Will 'borophene' replace graphene as a better conductor of electrons? |journal=Nature Communications |volume=5 |pages=3113 |doi=10.1038/ncomms4113 |pmid=24445427 |publisher=KurzweilAI |accessdate=2014-02-05|year=2014 |last1=Piazza |first1=Zachary A. |last2=Hu |first2=Han-Shi |last3=Li |first3=Wei-Li |last4=Zhao |first4=Ya-Fan |last5=Li |first5=Jun |last6=Wang |first6=Lai-Sheng |doi-access=free |bibcode=2014NatCo...5.3113P }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/ncomms4113|pmid=24445427|bibcode=2014NatCo...5.3113P| title = Planar hexagonal B<sub>36</sub> as a potential basis for extended single-atom layer boron sheets| journal = Nature Communications| volume = 5|article-number=3113| year = 2014| last1 = Piazza | first1 = Z. A. | last2 = Hu | first2 = H. S. | last3 = Li | first3 = W. L. | last4 = Zhao | first4 = Y. F. | last5 = Li | first5 = J. | last6 = Wang | first6 = L. S. | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Wang has published over 530 articles in publications including ''[[Nature Magazine]]'', ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'', ''[[Angewandte Chemie]]'', and the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]''.
